The alternatives are:

**2. Build the set with a loop instead of `secondArr.map(mapper)`**

This would skip creating an intermediate array, but the timing was not consistent: −10% in one run and +13% in the other. Speed alone doesn't justify it. There is a correctness reason, though, below.

## A bug I found along the way

`secondArr.map(mapper)` calls `mapper(item, index, array)`, but items from `firstArr` get `mapper(item)` only. So the two arrays can be mapped differently. I confirmed it:

```js
intersectionBy(['11'], ['0', '11'], parseInt) // → []  (expected ['11'])
// second array: parseInt('11', 1) → NaN;  first array: parseInt('11') → 11
```

The documented signature is `(item: T | U) => unknown`, so the second array shouldn't be getting an index and array. Building the set with an explicit loop (`mappedSecondSet.add(mapper(secondArr[i]))`) fixes it, and that's the real reason to make change 2.

## Suggested next step
